title: First-responder runtime sleuth and TF compatibility quickguide
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact first-responder guide for Private (VPC / on-prem) installs and upgrades. It focuses on common installation and runtime failure patterns we see in the field and quick probes you can run from the on-call laptop or bastion. Also contains condensed Terraform module compatibility notes and a safe upgrade checklist for fast decisioning when customers are on the line.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: first responders, SREs, installation engineers, and solutions engineers doing customer triage.
- Scope: bootstrap failures, TF apply/apply-hangs, node bootstrap, runtime model load / OOM, GPU/driver mismatches, networking & certificate boundaries, and quick pre/post-upgrade validations.

Immediate triage flow (0-15 mins):
1) Establish access and scope: can you reach the control-plane API and customer bastion? Which cluster (region/az) and deployment type (VPC vs on-prem)?
2) High-level status: check core services: redis, postgres, lighthouse/runtime-manager, envoy/pilot, and the node agents. If many services are DOWN, suspect install/terraform or networking.
3) Grab logs (see commands below) and copy them to a short paste or attach to Jira.
4) If install/upgrade is in progress, find the exact TF apply command or K8s rollout and pause escalation until we confirm whether it’s a transient lock/hang.

Quick commands (bastion or admin node) - safe and fast:
- Check connectivity: curl -fsS https://<api-host>/health || echo "api unreachable"
- Net test to model nodes: nc -vz <node-ip> 50051  (gRPC) and 443/80 for REST
- List failing pods: kubectl -n redwood get pods --field-selector status.phase!=Running -o wide
- Pod logs: kubectl -n redwood logs <pod> --tail=200 || kubectl -n redwood logs <pod> -c <container> --previous
- Node status: kubectl get nodes -o wide; ssh to node and journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 200
- GPU checks: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total,memory.used,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 2 (or check /var/log/nvidia-installer.log)
- Disk IO: iostat -x 1 3; df -h /var/lib/redwood
- Kernel/dmesg errors: sudo dmesg | tail -n 200  (look for firmware, iommu, driver oops)
- Time sync: timedatectl status; chronyc sourcestats -v or ntpq -p

Symptom-specific playbook (high-priority checks + likely remediations)

A) Terraform apply hangs or bootstrap never finishes
Signs: terraform apply stuck for >10min on resource creation, bootstrap step shows waiting for cloud-init forever, many K8s objects in Pending.
Quick probes:
- On workspace machine: ps aux | grep terraform, check terraform lock (terraform.tfstate.lock.info)
- Check remote state health (S3/GCS/consul): aws s3api head-object --bucket <tf-state-bucket> --key <state> or gsutil ls gs://bucket/state
- Inspect provider versions: grep "required_providers" -n modules/*/versions.tf
- Confirm service account perms: aws sts get-caller-identity; test IAM actions (iam:GetRole)
Common root causes and fixes:
- Provider plugin mismatch: run terraform init -upgrade and pin providers used by modules.
- State lock left by crashed flow: terraform force-unlock <LOCK-ID> only after confirming no concurrent applies.
- VPC/subnet CIDR overlap with customer network: verify module inputs; if overlap, update variables and replan with replacement (non-trivial—coordinate maintenance).
- Long cloud-init due to missing S3 access or proxy blocking: check cloud-init logs on instance (/var/log/cloud-init.log).

B) Services crash-looping post-install (e.g., runtime-manager, grpc-proxy)
Symptoms: pods in CrashLoopBackOff with exit codes 137, 134, or non-zero.
Probes:
- kubectl describe pod <pod> to get oom/killed events.
- logs: kubectl logs <pod> -c runtime --tail=300
- node memory: free -m; top -bn1 | head -n 20
Top hypotheses & mitigations:
- OOM due to model preloading: lower startup concurrency or use smaller model variant; edit Deployment resource to reduce replicas or request/limits.
- cgroups/oom_killer invoked because of mis-sized systemd slice: check systemd-cgls and tune kubelet/ECS settings.
- Permission denied to mount secrets (KMS/HSM): check CSI driver logs and KMS plugin credentials and node time sync.

C) Model fails to load or inference NPE / missing weights
Probes:
- runtime logs for model manager: grep -A30 "model load" /var/log/redwood/runtime.log
- Check model artifact path: ls -la /var/lib/redwood/models/<model-id>
- Verify download successes: http logs from artifact store or s3 get-object --bucket <bucket> --key <model>
Hypotheses and fixes:
- Corrupt artifacts (partial upload): re-pull artifact or re-run model push with checksum verification.
- Wrong quantization/profile used for hardware (e.g., bf16-only model on int8 runtime): use compatible model variant or enable fallback to FP16.
- KV cache eviction causing OOM during load: increase node memory or reduce initial batch size for warmup.

D) GPU driver / CUDA mismatch or MIG issues
Probes:
- nvidia-smi; check driver version and compare with runtime-supported list (see module README / driver matrix)
- journalctl -u nvidia-container-runtime or dmesg for UVM errors
Remediations:
- If driver < required: schedule maintenance to update driver and reboot nodes; for immediate relief, move pods to nodes with compatible drivers.
- For MIG shape/partitioning mismatches: ensure runtime flags match configured MIG profiles; restart device-plugin after MIG change.

E) Network / TLS / certificate failures (envoy, grpc TLS handshake errors)
Probes:
- curl -v https://<service-host>:<port>/health --cacert <ca.pem>
- openssl s_client -connect <host>:<port> -servername <host>
- iptables -L -n; verify host-level firewall and security groups
Common fixes:
- Wrong CA/expiry: rotate certs, ensure control-plane and nodes trust the same CA bundle.
- MTU/path-mtu causing gRPC stalls: check if MTU differs between customer network and node host; set LOWER_MTU env var (1400) on envoy and host route.

Terraform module compatibility notes (short, practical)
- Always pin module and provider versions in production stacks. Floating to latest provider often introduces API changes that break apply.
- Keep the module upgrade window: when bumping module major versions, run a plan in a staging account with identical variable sets and tfstate snapshot.
- Remote state format: adding new resources that replace identifiers may require state mv; include state mv steps in upgrade notes.
- Provider aliasing: if the install uses aliased providers for multi-region, ensure module inputs accept provider aliases (most of our modules include provider = aws.myalias).
- Sensitive data: avoid committing KMS keys or ARNs inside modules; pass them via variables and secrets backend.
Common tf pitfalls observed in customer installs:
- module input defaults that assume large CIDR blocks (-> conflict). Always review vars.tf before apply.
- Race between node bootstrapping and cloud-init attaching volumes (attach/detach loops): add retry/backoff in user-data scripts and ensure volumes exist in same AZ.

Upgrade checklist (preflight -> canary -> full)
Preflight (72–1 hour before):
- Create backups: snapshot Postgres, S3/GCS model artifact buckets, and terraform state snapshot.
- Record baseline metrics: tail -n 100 redwood runtime logs, collect GPU utilization and average 95p latency for last 24h.
- Validate tf plan in staging with same variables and tfstate snapshot.
Canary phase (small % of qps or single node):
- Drain a single node: cordon + drain + replace runtime container image or module change.
- Run validation scripts: make sure /health passes; run sample generation sequence that asserts on exact token count and latency threshold.
- Monitor for 15–30 minutes for memory growth, OOMs, slow tails. If anomalies, revert.
Full rollout:
- Rolling update with pause windows; watch for spikes in 95p latency and token error rates.
- Post-rollout: run the full smoke test suite and keep rollback plan ready for 2 hours.
Rollback triggers (examples):
- Regressed 95p latency by >25% vs baseline for >15 minutes
- New OOMs observed across >15% of nodes or crashloops that don’t stabilize within the pause window
- Persistent TLS handshake errors to core services

Post-upgrade smoke tests (quick list)
- API health: curl -sS https://<api>/health (expect 200 + JSON status OK)
- Small generation: POST /v1/generate with a short prompt, expect successful streaming tokens within SLA latency
- Embeddings: hit embedding endpoint and verify cosine distance between two test vectors is expected range
- Model warmup: request warmup profile and verify KV cache size increased without eviction errors in logs
- Resource checks: run nvidia-smi and ensure GPUs are in use and driver versions match matrix

Escalation and context capture (what to include in ticket/Slack):
- Deployment id / TF workspace / commit hash for modules and runtime image
- Exact timestamps, node IPs, pod names, and the first error seen in logs
- Outputs of the quick commands listed above and a short summary: "what changed (upgrade/terraform change), observed impact, immediate mitigation attempted"

Contact / channels:
- #onprem-ops (pagerduty routing via eng-onprem), primary on-call: Marco Hernandez
- SRE lead: Eun-ji Kim
- Solutions engineer: Liam O'Neill

Notes to self / future TODOs:
- Add a short python script to automate the quick smoke checks and gather logs into a single tarball for upload.
- Add TF preflight validator that checks for CIDR overlap and provider mismatches before any apply completes.
- Consolidate driver matrix into module README and surface it in the Console for Private customers.

Appendix: quick hypothesis checklist (tickboxes for first responder)
- [ ] Can reach control plane API
- [ ] TF state healthy and unlocked
- [ ] No major node OOMs in last 30min
- [ ] GPUs present and drivers match required matrix
- [ ] Certificates valid (not expired)
- [ ] MTU mismatch ruled out
- [ ] Artifact store reachable and model pulls succeed

End of guide. Keep this short guide as the fast-path for escalation; add links to longer playbooks for deep-dive forensic steps.
